title: Bob Dylan
label: Columbia
note: Recorded in two afternoons for $402. Only two originals; the rest are the songs a 20-year-old carried out of the Village coffeehouses.

tracks.t: Baby, Let Me Follow You Down

tracks.note: A tribute to Woody Guthrie, sung to the tune of Guthrie's own '1913 Massacre'.

tracks.t: See That My Grave Is Kept Clean

title: The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan
label: Columbia
note: The album that made him. Eleven originals, written in a single astonishing year.

tracks.note: Written in about ten minutes in April 1962, reputedly at the Commons on MacDougal Street. Peter, Paul and Mary took it to No. 2.
Borrows from 'Scarborough Fair', which Martin Carthy had taught him in London.
Set to the melody of the English folk song 'Nottamun Town'.
Every line, he said, was the first line of a song he thought he'd never have time to write.

tracks.t: Don't Think Twice, It's All Right
tracks.note: Melody adapted from Paul Clayton's 'Who's Gonna Buy You Ribbons'.
About James Meredith's enrollment at the University of Mississippi.

tracks.t: Honey, Just Allow Me One More Chance

title: The Times They Are a-Changin'
label: Columbia
note: His starkest record: ten originals, no humor, no covers, guitar and harmonica and the weight of the world.

tracks.note: Deliberately written as an anthem, drawing on Scottish and Irish ballad cadences.
Melody from Dominic Behan's 'The Patriot Game'.
Sung from the viewpoint of a miner's wife in the Iron Range where he grew up.

tracks.t: Only a Pawn in Their Game
tracks.note: About the murder of Medgar Evers. Dylan sang it at the March on Washington.
Written in a fit of pique after a hotel clerk refused him a room.

tracks.t: The Lonesome Death of Hattie Carroll
tracks.note: Drawn almost line for line from a Baltimore newspaper report.
Melody from the Irish 'The Parting Glass'. He sang it to Frank Sinatra at Sinatra's 80th birthday, by request.

title: Another Side of Bob Dylan
label: Columbia
note: Recorded in one night with a bottle of Beaujolais. The protest singer walks offstage; the poet walks on.

tracks.t: All I Really Want to Do

tracks.note: The first Dylan recording on which he plays piano.
Partly written in the back of a station wagon on a cross-country drive in February 1964.
'I was so much older then, I'm younger than that now.' A farewell to finger-pointing songs.

tracks.t: I Don't Believe You (She Acts Like We Never Have Met)

tracks.note: About the end of his relationship with Suze Rotolo. He later called writing it a mistake.

title: Bringing It All Back Home
label: Columbia
note: One side electric, one side acoustic. The hinge of the whole decade.

tracks.note: His first Top 40 hit in the US. The cue-card film clip is among the first music videos.
Opened the electric set at Newport in July 1965.
Begins with a false start and Dylan collapsing in laughter, left on the record on purpose.
The Byrds' version became the first folk-rock No. 1.
'He not busy being born is busy dying.' Quoted by Jimmy Carter in his 1976 acceptance speech.

tracks.t: It's All Over Now, Baby Blue
tracks.note: The last song he played at Newport 1965, acoustic, after the electric set.

title: Highway 61 Revisited
label: Columbia
note: Named for the road that runs from his Minnesota hometown down to the Delta. Rock music grew up here.

tracks.note: Cut from a twenty-page 'long piece of vomit'. Al Kooper, not a keyboard player, improvised the organ part. Rolling Stone's greatest song of all time.

tracks.t: It Takes a Lot to Laugh, It Takes a Train to Cry

tracks.note: 'Something is happening here, but you don't know what it is, do you, Mister Jones?'
The police-siren whistle was Dylan's own.
Eleven minutes, acoustic, with Charlie McCoy's Spanish guitar. Einstein disguised as Robin Hood, Ezra Pound and T.S. Eliot fighting in the captain's tower.

title: Blonde on Blonde
label: Columbia
note: Rock's first double album, cut mostly in Nashville with session players in overnight marathons. 'That thin, that wild mercury sound.'

tracks.note: Cut late at night with a Salvation Army-style brass band. 'Everybody must get stoned.'
Many critics' pick for his finest lyric. 'The ghost of 'lectricity howls in the bones of her face.'

tracks.t: One of Us Must Know (Sooner or Later)
Stuck Inside of Mobile with the Memphis Blues Again
Most Likely You Go Your Way and I'll Go Mine

tracks.note: 'To live outside the law, you must be honest.'
Widely heard as an answer to the Beatles' 'Norwegian Wood'.
Fills the entire fourth side. Written, he later sang, for his wife Sara.

title: John Wesley Harding
label: Columbia
note: After the motorcycle crash: twelve spare parables, recorded in Nashville in about twelve hours, released into the Summer of Love's psychedelic hangover.

tracks.note: The real outlaw spelled his name Hardin. Dylan said the extra 'g' was a mistake.

tracks.t: As I Went Out One Morning
I Dreamed I Saw St. Augustine
tracks.note: Modeled on the labor hymn 'I Dreamed I Saw Joe Hill Last Night'.
Jimi Hendrix's version arrived within months. Dylan has since performed it more than any other song of his, and plays it Hendrix's way.

tracks.t: The Ballad of Frankie Lee and Judas Priest

tracks.note: A preview of the country croon to come.

title: Nashville Skyline
label: Columbia
note: Twenty-seven minutes of country contentment, sung in a new, smooth voice he attributed to quitting cigarettes.

tracks.note: Duet with Johnny Cash, from sessions that produced an album's worth of duets, finally released on the Bootleg Series in 2019.
An instrumental.
Written for 'Midnight Cowboy' but delivered too late for the film. His biggest hit in years.

tracks.t: Tell Me That It Isn't True
Tonight I'll Be Staying Here with You

title: Self Portrait
label: Columbia
note: A sprawling double album of covers, instrumentals and live cuts. Greil Marcus's review began: 'What is this shit?' Dylan later said he made it to shake off the cult.

tracks.note: Two lines, sung by a female chorus, repeated for three minutes. Dylan does not sing.

tracks.t: I Forgot More Than You'll Ever Know

tracks.w: Gilbert Bécaud / Pierre Delanoë / Mann Curtis

tracks.note: An instrumental.
Live at the Isle of Wight, 1969, with The Band.
Dylan double-tracks himself, singing both Simon and Garfunkel's parts.
Live at the Isle of Wight, 1969.

tracks.t: Take Me as I Am (Or Let Me Go)

tracks.note: Live at the Isle of Wight, 1969.
Live at the Isle of Wight, 1969.
Wordless humming over a mariachi horn section. A Top 50 single.

title: New Morning
label: Columbia
note: Released four months after Self Portrait, to relief. Dylan at the piano, domestic and warm.

tracks.note: George Harrison recorded it too, on 'All Things Must Pass'; Olivia Newton-John had the hit.
About receiving an honorary doctorate from Princeton in June 1970, as the cicadas screamed.
Possibly about a meeting with Elvis Presley in Las Vegas, which may or may not have happened.
A jazz-club recitation with scat vocals from Maeretha Stewart.
Revived decades later by 'The Big Lebowski'.

title: Pat Garrett & Billy the Kid
label: Columbia
note: Soundtrack to Sam Peckinpah's western, in which Dylan also appears as the knife-throwing Alias.

tracks.note: An instrumental.
An instrumental.
An instrumental.
Wordless vocals.
An instrumental, with Byron Berline's fiddle.
Written for the scene where Slim Pickens' sheriff dies by the river. Covered by nearly everyone since.
An instrumental.

title: Dylan
label: Columbia
note: Outtakes from Self Portrait and New Morning, released by Columbia without his involvement after he left for Asylum. Long kept out of print.

tracks.w: George David Weiss / Hugo Peretti / Luigi Creatore

title: Planet Waves
label: Asylum
note: His first No. 1 album, recorded with The Band in three days before their 1974 tour.

tracks.note: Written as a lullaby for one of his sons. The album includes it twice, slow and fast, because he couldn't choose.

title: Blood on the Tracks
label: Columbia
note: Recorded in New York, then half re-recorded in Minneapolis over Christmas. 'A lot of people tell me they enjoy that album. It's hard for me to relate to that.'

tracks.note: Written, he said, like a painting, with past and present on the same canvas. He still rewrites its verses onstage.
'Blowing every time you move your teeth.' The New York version is a whisper; the released Minneapolis take is a snarl.

tracks.t: You're Gonna Make Me Lonesome When You Go
Lily, Rosemary and the Jack of Hearts
tracks.note: A fifteen-verse western in which the cabaret, the bank and the hanging judge all have their moment.

tracks.t: If You See Her, Say Hello

title: The Basement Tapes
label: Columbia
note: Recorded in 1967 in the basement of Big Pink in West Saugerties and bootlegged for years before this official release. Only Dylan's songs are shown here; The Band's own tracks are omitted.

tracks.note: A deadpan answer to Bobbie Gentry's 'Ode to Billie Joe'.

tracks.t: Yea! Heavy and a Bottle of Bread
Crash on the Levee (Down in the Flood)

tracks.note: The Byrds opened 'Sweetheart of the Rodeo' with it.
